summary.text: The Local Group is the galaxy group that includes the Milky Way, shaped like a dumbbell with the Milky Way and its satellites at one end and the Andromeda Galaxy and its satellites at the other.
The two halves are about 800 kiloparsecs apart and are moving toward one another at 123 km/s.
It has 134 known members, most of them dwarf galaxies, and it belongs to the Virgo Supercluster, which is part of the Laniakea Supercluster.

facts.label: Shape
facts.value: Dumbbell with two lobes, each with satellites

facts.label: Known members
facts.value: 134 within one megaparsec, mostly dwarf galaxies

facts.label: Name introduced
facts.value: By Edwin Hubble in his 1936 book

items.prompt: Imagine the Local Group as a dumbbell. What sits at its two ends?

options.label: Andromeda with its satellites, and the Triangulum Galaxy alone
Our galaxy with its satellites, and Andromeda with its own
The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds with their neighbours
Our galaxy with its satellites, and the Triangulum Galaxy

items.explain: The Milky Way and its satellites form one lobe, and the Andromeda Galaxy and its satellites form the other.

items.prompt: Astronomers can give only a current total of galaxies in our local group, not an exact number. What is the reason?

options.label: Dwarf galaxies are too far away to detect
Galaxies merge so often that the count changes daily
Our own galaxy blocks the view of some
Most galaxies there give off no light

items.explain: The exact number is unknown because the Milky Way obscures some of the galaxies.

items.prompt: Gravity is pulling the Local Group's galaxies together. Over tens of billions of years, what is the group likely to become?

options.label: A bigger collection of many separate spiral galaxies
One elliptical galaxy, led by Andromeda and our galaxy merging
A wider scatter as all of its galaxies drift apart
A group that stays exactly as it is today for good

items.explain: The galaxies are likely to merge into a single elliptical galaxy, with the Andromeda and Milky Way merger the main event.

items.prompt: The Triangulum Galaxy once passed close to Andromeda, 2 to 4 billion years ago. What did that encounter do?

options.label: Merged the two galaxies into one
Stripped Andromeda of its satellites
Tore Triangulum into a stream of stars
Triggered star formation across Andromeda's disk

items.explain: The close passage triggered star formation across Andromeda's disk.

items.prompt: Pick a known member of the Local Group at random. What is it most likely to be?

options.label: A dwarf galaxy
A giant spiral like Andromeda
A supergiant elliptical
A galaxy larger than the Milky Way

items.explain: Most of the 134 known members are dwarf galaxies.

items.prompt: The Pisces Dwarf Galaxy sits equally far from the Andromeda Galaxy and the Triangulum Galaxy. What can astronomers say about it?

options.label: It belongs to the Milky Way's lobe
It cannot be a satellite of any galaxy
It may be a satellite of either
It is certainly Andromeda's satellite

items.explain: Because it is equidistant from both, it may be a satellite of either.
